hero_title: The World Cup like never before
hero_deck: AccreditaPass tells press teams what their accreditation allows across the tournament, from approval to the final whistle.
hero_role1: Roles — UX researcher · Product designer · Front-end developer
hero_role3: Scope — UX research → UX design → prototyping → development
hero_rv_txt: 104 matches, 16 stadiums and three countries, with no guarantee a press pass is valid for every match. Venues change, spaces shrink and knockout quotas hang on a goal nobody has scored. Without timely notice, journalists run into reality at the stadium gate. AccreditaPass removes that friction: a personal record that shows what changed, why, and the action plan for the best coverage.
act1_lede: Four failures that turn a valid pass into a wasted trip.
p1_x: Access withdrawn without a reason breaks the journalist's logistics and leaves no way to respond.
p1_r: A journalist prepares the kit, plans the coverage and meets a closed gate with nobody behind it. The simulated research rounds found that a refusal with a clear reason is manageable: it can be appealed, worked around or turned into a new angle. A silent one leaves the journalist in the dark. It falls hardest on freelancers and small outlets, who end up relying on corridor talk instead of an official answer.
p2_x: Access changes travel slowly and surface when the pass fails outside the stadium.
p2_r: Teams go out and press positions are reassigned between matchdays: that is the nature of the tournament. The failure is when the paperwork moves slower than the journalist. A reporter pays for a flight, rushes to the stadium and is held twenty minutes before kickoff because gate staff are reading an outdated list. The problem is never the change itself, but the delay in telling the person already standing at the barrier.
p3_x: Many learn the hard way that an approved accreditation does not guarantee getting through the turnstiles.
p3_r: It is usually learned at the worst moment: a press credential does not automatically secure entry to the venue. Even veterans who read the fine print get caught by it. One plain line on the confirmation itself would spare the turnstile surprise and save both the day's coverage and the reporter's standing.
p4_x: A journalist needs to know the real conditions of knockout-round coverage before buying a flight.
p4_r: In the knockout rounds everything hangs on the next win. Quarter-final and final positions depend on matches not yet played. When the rules sound settled, a logistical possibility passes for a promise that will break. Stated as conditions from the first day, they would let journalists book flights and hotels on what is likely, not on costly assumptions.
act2_lede: The design research runs that turned doubts into decisions before any code.
l1_x: A journalist can take bad news; what breaks trust is no explanation and late notice.
l1_r: Eight stages took the research to a design brief. Simulated survey and interview data, declared as such, and a service blueprint mapped the journalist's journey through tournament coverage. Three problems stood out: institutional silence, late notice, and the belief that a credential equals entry.
l2_x: Every change shows what changed, why, and what to do next, delivered before it hurts.
l2_r: A simulated two-day workshop produced 32 ideas, narrowed through feasibility and prioritisation matrices to a ranked shortlist of eight. The concept that won syncs each update between the journalist and gate staff at once, and scales how much each person hears to how much help they already have.
l3_x: Flows and screens were locked first, so dev followed a solid structure rather than a guess.
l3_r: Nine stages turned the concept into a build-ready specification: an information architecture from a simulated card sort, design tokens verified against WCAG 2.2 AA in light and dark, task flows and a data model. It also settled sign-in and support for three languages.
act2_question: How might we soften the impact of an access change on journalists?
hmw_a_x: Turn accreditation into a live record: every change reaches the journalist and the venue gate in real time, with its reason and the next step.
sch_verdict: Five weeks, right after the final.
sch_lede: Seven phases from sketch to finished build.
gantt_noscript: This chart draws from its data with JavaScript.
sch_note: Reconstructed from the public commit history of github.com/jdsaire/accreditapass: 206 commits across 16 runs, 28 Jul – 30 Aug 2026. The research, ideation and specification dossiers were written outside the repository, so their bars mark the day each one entered it. Nothing was committed from 1 to 10 August or from 21 to 28 August.
act4_lede: The four pillars that hold the build's architecture together.
b1_x: The app lives entirely client-side, so a journalist can open it on any phone without depending on a server behind it.
b1_r: Blazor WebAssembly on .NET 10, written in C#, with a narrow TypeScript layer of two files for theme and locale storage. The app runs on an in-memory provider behind one interface, so every page reads the mock or the API without changing a line. Seven routes; the record is gated because it is personal, while the match schedule and help stay public. English, Spanish and Portuguese run at exact parity, 339 keys each, and switching language or theme never signs you out.
b2_x: When something changes, the record updates on its own, with no refresh and no support call.
b2_r: An ASP.NET Core Web API with validated CRUD endpoints and an in-memory store, switched off by default so the live site never depends on it. Its middleware runs in a stated order: CORS, error handling, token authentication, request logging. SignalR carries each change notification to the client. It is a basic layer that proves the contract, not a production back end.
b3_x: Every screen shares one set of design tokens, tuned for a light and a dark theme.
b3_r: Dual-theme design tokens were defined in the prototyping round and verified against WCAG 2.2 AA in both themes. The dark palette was re-derived against a #000000 anchor rather than inverted. The access card, change row, foreseeable badge and stale indicator share one token set, and appearance follows a three-way setting: light, dark or system.
b4_x: Smooth keyboard navigation and screen-reader support, passing more than twice the accessibility checks it started with.
b4_r: A new change is announced to assistive technology the moment it happens. Skip links, visible focus at all times and clear labels with input validation are built in. To avoid flooding screen readers, help sections and change rows use progressive disclosure, showing detail only when the user asks for it.
act5_lede: Compare the results across three kinds of test.
act5_t1_r: Audit 1: 26 findings. Moving from editable forms to read-only EventCards resolved half of the critical findings; labelled inputs and relative links closed the rest, alongside 15 fixes across major and minor findings. Audit 2 raised one new critical (false "Access withdrawn" states on unplayed matches), fixed in v13 by bounding status to changes already in effect, a release that also shipped the withdraw action and aria-live announcements for new changes. v13 was not re-audited.
act5_t2_r: From 5 fails at the first evaluation to 7 passes at the second. Match with the real world (read-only cards), recognition over recall (previous values in view) and flexibility (search, filters and skip links) now pass, as do error prevention and error recovery. User control and consistency were addressed in v13, which lets pending requests be withdrawn and unifies how their status is displayed, without a re-audit.
act5_t3_r: From 12 initial fails to 18 passes. Fixes covered explicit label-for pairing, skip links, visible focus rings, alert roles for errors and recomputed contrast (up to 8.32:1 in dark mode). The one remaining fail (4.1.3, on the conditional status) was fixed in v13. Target size, reflow at 320 px and the Spanish sign-out row stay open because neither audit ran in a browser.
act5_footnote_audits: Audit 1 measured the pre-reframing app at commit 0653b4e. Audit 2 measured the build at b37066d. Both used simulated task-attempts and participants; neither involved a real user.
act5_footnote_disposition: All 26 first-audit findings got a disposition: 18 fixed, 5 not applicable, 2 open and 1 partly fixed.
act5_footnote_tests: 512 front-end and 33 back-end automated tests, in xUnit and bUnit.
act6_verdict: What this app lets me say.
act6_lede: What it solved, where its technical limits sit, and what comes next.
r1_x: I conceived, designed and shipped this interface in a stack I had never used, directing the code and debugging it until it held.
r2_x: The data store, sign-in and server run as a proof of concept: enough to prove the product logic, not built for production.
r3_x: Next, I bring this end-to-end way of building to the digital team of an established company, as an AI Product & Experience Engineer.
disclosure1_body: No affiliation, endorsement or institutional link with FIFA. Accreditation data runs as a local simulation in the browser session and is never stored. The match schedule is the only real asset.
disclosure2_body: The studies documented here involved no real users. Every dataset, workshop participant and usability test is a synthetic artifact created to demonstrate the method, not the result of recruitment.
